what_its_for: Adalimumab-adaz is used to reduce pain, swelling, and inflammation caused by certain immune system conditions. It is approved to treat rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis (spine inflammation), Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, plaque psoriasis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and uveitis (eye inflammation). It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes inflammation.
how_to_take: This medicine comes as a liquid injection given under the skin (subcutaneous injection). It is available as a prefilled syringe or an autoinjector pen. Common injection sites include the front of your thighs or your belly (abdomen), at least 2 inches away from your belly button. Rotate your injection sites each time and never inject into skin that is tender, bruised, red, hard, or scarred. Take the medicine out of the refrigerator about 15 to 30 minutes before injecting to let it reach room temperature, which makes the injection more comfortable. A healthcare provider will teach you how to inject yourself properly before you do it on your own.
dosing: Your dose depends on the condition being treated. For most adult conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, the typical dose is 40 mg injected every other week. For Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, your doctor may start you on a higher dose (called a loading dose) and then switch you to 40 mg every other week. For plaque psoriasis, the starting dose may be 80 mg, followed by 40 mg every other week. Children's doses are based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose and schedule.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember. Then continue on your regular schedule from that new date. Do not inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store adalimumab-adaz in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it, and do not use it if it has been frozen. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 14 days, but once removed from the refrigerator and kept at room temperature, use it within 14 days or throw it away. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of used syringes and pens in an FDA-approved sharps disposal container right away after use.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as the live flu nasal spray, shingles vaccine Zostavax, or yellow fever vaccine) while taking this medicine, as they could cause serious infections. Avoid close contact with people who have active infections, especially tuberculosis (TB), chickenpox, or other contagious illnesses. Avoid drinking excessive amounts of alcohol, which can stress your immune system further. Do not start this medication if you have an active infection without talking to your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, persistent cough, shortness of breath, painful or burning urination, or open sores on your skin; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; vision changes; chest pain or shortness of breath; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also tell your doctor before any surgery or dental procedure.
when_it_works: You may begin to notice some improvement in your symptoms within 2 to 4 weeks after starting treatment. However, it may take up to 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefits of this medication. It is important to keep taking it as prescribed even if you do not notice immediate improvement. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It may be used during pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks, but your baby may need special monitoring after birth. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of this medicine may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine can be used in children for certain conditions such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and uveitis. The dose is based on the child's weight. Elderly: Older adults may have a higher risk of infections. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Immunocompromised patients: If your immune system is already weakened due to another condition or medication, let your doctor know, as you may be at higher risk for serious infections.
